provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Padgett v. Department of Health & Rehabilitative Services
key_cases.holding: Parental rights may be involuntarily terminated only on clear and convincing proof that reunification poses a substantial risk of significant harm to the child and that termination is the least restrictive means of protecting the child, which ordinarily requires a good-faith agency effort to rehabilitate the parent and reunite the family; abuse of one child may supply grounds as to another child.
key_cases.relevance: This is Florida's controlling standard for involuntary termination of parental rights and the source of the least-restrictive-means test.
key_cases.quote: the state must show by clear and convincing evidence that reunification with the parent poses a substantial risk of significant harm to the child

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Before a State may sever completely and irrevocably the rights of parents in their natural child, due process requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence; New York's fair-preponderance standard was unconstitutional.
key_cases.relevance: It is the constitutional source of Florida's clear-and-convincing standard for termination of parental rights.
key_cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.case_name: S.M. v. Florida Department of Children & Families
key_cases.holding: Once grounds for termination are proved by clear and convincing evidence and reunification is not in the child's manifest best interests, the least-restrictive-means requirement does not oblige the trial court to consider permanent guardianship instead of adoption.
key_cases.relevance: S.M. confirms that adoption outranks guardianship once termination grounds are established, limiting the least-restrictive-means argument.
key_cases.quote: Section 39.621, Florida Statutes (2016), specifies that permanent guardianship shall be considered only after reunification and adoption are not available options.

key_cases.case_name: J.B. v. Florida Department of Children & Families
key_cases.holding: An indigent parent's right to counsel in termination proceedings includes the right to effective assistance and a procedural means of raising such claims, although J.B. herself showed no basis to set aside the termination order.
key_cases.relevance: This decision creates the ineffective-assistance remedy that now accompanies every Florida termination judgment against an indigent parent.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the right to counsel in termination of parental right (TPR) proceedings includes the right to effective assistance and requires a means of vindicating that right

key_cases.case_name: Statewide Guardian ad Litem Office v. C.C.
key_cases.holding: An appellate court may not reweigh the evidence supporting a termination judgment; because competent substantial evidence supported the trial court's least-restrictive-means and manifest-best-interests findings after the father failed a voluntary case plan, the district court's reversal was quashed.
key_cases.relevance: C.C. is the most recent Florida Supreme Court statement on proof of least restrictive means and manifest best interests in termination cases.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the Fifth District's decision improperly reweighed the evidence below and, thus, conflicts with our precedent.

key_cases.holding: Indigent parents have a constitutional right to appointed counsel whenever the proceeding can result in permanent loss of parental custody; in other dependency proceedings the right is determined case by case.
key_cases.relevance: D.B. is Florida's foundational right-to-counsel holding for proceedings ending in permanent severance.
key_cases.quote: We find that a constitutional right to counsel necessarily arises where the proceedings can result in permanent loss of parental custody.
